content: The document titled Recommendations and Guidance on Hepatitis C Virus Self-Testing (July 2021) provides a detailed analysis of the cost-effectiveness of self-testing for hepatitis C virus (HCV). It was authored by Josephine G. Walker, Philippa Easterbrook, Emmanuel Fajardo, Elena Ivanova, Muhammad S. Jamil, Cheryl Johnson, Niklas Luhmann, Jason J. Ong, Fern Terris-Prestholt, Peter Vickerman, and Sonjelle Shilton, among others. The publication is copyrighted by the World Health Organization (WHO) and is available under a Creative Commons license for non-commercial use, provided proper citation is given. The document emphasizes that HCV infection is a significant global health issue, with an estimated 58 million people infected worldwide in 2021. However, only 26% of these individuals were aware of their diagnosis. HCV self-testing (HCVST) has been proposed as a strategy to improve access to testing and increase awareness of HCV status. Self-testing involves individuals collecting their own specimens, performing a rapid diagnostic test (RDT), and interpreting the results themselves. This approach has been successfully implemented for HIV self-testing (HIVST), which has been recommended by WHO since 2016 and is now widely adopted in 88 countries. The study models the cost per HCV diagnosis and cure using HCVST compared to traditional facility-based testing. It focuses on four case studies representing different populations and prevalence levels: men who have sex with men (MSM) in China, men aged 40–49 in Georgia, people who inject drugs (PWID) in Vietnam, and PWID in Kenya. The analysis uses a decision-tree model with a one-year time horizon to evaluate the economic cost from a provider's perspective, reported as incremental cost per patient diagnosed or cured. Key findings include: 1. HCVST increases the total number of people tested, diagnosed, and cured, but at a higher cost compared to standard testing. The cost per diagnosis with self-testing is higher than standard care, with incremental costs varying by setting: $104 in Vietnam, $163 in Georgia, $587 in Kenya, and $2,647 in China. These differences are driven by variations in HCV prevalence and other factors. 2. Sensitivity analyses show that reducing the cost of oral-fluid-based self-tests, switching to cheaper blood-based self-tests, increasing uptake of HCVST, and improving linkage to care can reduce the cost per diagnosis in all settings. 3. The incremental cost per cure is lowest in Georgia ($1,418), followed by Vietnam ($2,033), Kenya ($2,566), and highest in China ($4,956). These costs are influenced by treatment costs and other factors. The study highlights that introducing HCVST is more cost-effective in populations with high HCV prevalence. However, the total cost of increased case-finding is also impacted by the cost of HCV treatment in each setting. The findings underscore the importance of considering cost-effectiveness and affordability when implementing HCVST alongside standard testing services. The WHO-recommended testing pathway for HCV begins with serological testing using an RDT or laboratory-based immunoassay, followed by confirmatory testing with HCV RNA nucleic acid testing (NAT) or core antigen testing to confirm active infection (viraemia). HCVST can be used as a screening test, followed by additional serological testing and confirmatory NAT or core antigen testing for those with reactive results. The study explores different self-testing models, including peer-guided self-testing for PWID in Kenya and Vietnam, and evaluates alternative pathways such as direct linkage to confirmatory NAT testing for viraemic infection. The decision-tree model represents three pathways: standard care testing, no testing, and self-testing. It incorporates differences in costs, resource use, and linkage to care rates across the four case study settings. The document concludes that while HCVST increases the number of people diagnosed and linked to care, it is associated with higher costs compared to standard testing. Policymakers and healthcare providers must decide on the implementation of HCVST, considering the target populations, testing pathways, and cost-effectiveness. The findings will inform WHO guidance on HCVST, alongside systematic reviews, usability studies, and qualitative assessments of values and preferences.
